title: TCS Probes Employee Data Exposure as Cybersecurity Pressures Mount After String of Client Breaches
excerpt: India's largest IT services firm says threat-intelligence alerts flagged possible exposure of older employee records, though no customer systems were compromised.
body:
• TCS disclosed on August 10 that it received threat-intelligence alerts about possible exposure of employee-related data, but found no evidence of customer system compromise.
  • The alleged data appears more than four years old and is limited to basic employee details; the attacker reportedly used password spraying and MFA fatigue techniques.
  • The disclosure comes after TCS dealt with cyberattacks on three major clients — Jaguar Land Rover, Marks & Spencer, and Co-operative Group — within a single year.
  • TCS is now forming six dedicated cybersecurity teams totaling 150 people to standardize security protocols for its largest clients.

What Happened

Tata Consultancy Services disclosed in a regulatory filing on August 10 that it had received threat-intelligence alerts alleging the possible exposure of certain employee-related data. India's largest IT services firm said its investigation found no credible evidence of a breach involving TCS systems or customer environments.

https://x.com/algotradingdesk/status/2089214798642958381

"The Company has investigated the matter and has not found any credible evidence of a breach of TCS systems or customer environments," TCS stated in its filing to the stock exchange.

According to TCS, the information referenced in the alerts appears to be more than four years old and is limited to basic employee-related details. The alleged attacker claimed to have used techniques such as password spraying and multi-factor authentication fatigue to gain access, but TCS said it has had safeguards against such methods for more than two years.

A Year of Cybersecurity Challenges

The disclosure arrives at a difficult time for TCS. Over the past year, three major clients — British retailers Marks & Spencer and Co-operative Group, and luxury automaker Jaguar Land Rover — have been hit by cyberattacks, all while relying on TCS for backend IT services.

"Recent incidents saw some of TCS's clients becoming victims to these cyber-attacks resulting in severe disruptions to their businesses. I would like to clarify that there has been no compromise of TCS systems, nor any impact to other customers in all these incidents."

— Aarthi Subramaniam, TCS Chief Operating Officer

The JLR breach proved the most damaging. Attackers identified as Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters infiltrated JLR's IT systems in August through compromised third-party employee identities and an unsecured SAP server, according to Livemint. The attack lasted roughly 45 days, halting car production, exposing employee and contractor payroll data, and causing a $150 million exceptional loss for the carmaker. Independent analysts estimate the total cost could exceed $1 billion.

TCS signed a five-year, $1 billion IT transformation deal with JLR in September 2023 covering cloud migration, cybersecurity, and application development. While TCS has maintained that attackers did not enter through its systems, the series of incidents has prompted a comprehensive reassessment of its cybersecurity posture.

Standardized Security Push

In response, TCS is piloting standardized cybersecurity practices for its largest clients. The company is forming six dedicated teams — approximately 150 people total — to develop and run fixed response procedures aimed at limiting damage from cyberattacks, according to Livemint.

These procedures include video validation of employees managing IT support functions, AI-powered tools to track hacker movement within systems, and additional network security layers. TCS plans to demonstrate the results of these pilots to all clients and then incorporate the protocols into their IT infrastructure.

The situation has drawn close attention from Tata Group leadership. TCS COO Aarthi Subramaniam, Tata Sons chief digital officer Aparna Ganesh, and TCS UK vice-president Sudeep Mazumdar have been providing weekly updates to Tata Sons chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran.

Industry-Wide Implications

For the Indian IT services industry, which manages critical digital infrastructure for enterprises worldwide, the episode underscores the growing complexity of cybersecurity risk management. TCS handles technology operations for some of the world's largest companies, and the reputational stakes of client breaches extend well beyond immediate financial losses.

Legal experts warn that incidents like the JLR breach could trigger multi-jurisdictional scrutiny across the UK, US, and India, with potential regulatory fines under UK GDPR reaching up to £17.5 million or 4% of global turnover. Class-action lawsuits from affected employees are also a risk, particularly in the US.

What's Next

TCS said it continues to closely monitor its systems and will take additional action if new information emerges regarding the employee data exposure. For the broader IT services sector, the company's cybersecurity pilot program — once proven — could set new standards for how outsourcing firms manage client security risk, especially as regulatory expectations tighten globally.

TCS reported revenue of $30.18 billion last fiscal year, with operating margins of 24.3%. The company faces headwinds from slowing growth and competitive pressure, making the restoration of client confidence an operational priority.
